say: You give it a double inequality with $x$ in the middle, like $-5 \le 2x + 3 < 9$. It gives back one **interval** for $x$.
The key idea: there are three parts, and whatever you do to one part you do to all three. The $x$ ends up alone in the middle.

steps.title: Subtract 3 from every part
steps.say: The $x$ is stuck with a $+3$. Subtract $3$ from all three parts, so the inequality stays balanced.

steps.title: Divide every part by 2
steps.say: Now divide all three parts by $2$. It is positive, so the signs stay the same way round.

lines.text: Dividing by a negative number would flip the signs. Here it does not.

steps.title: Read the interval
steps.say: $x$ is at least $\hl{1}{-4}$ and less than $\hl{2}{3}$. A $\le$ includes the end point, a $<$ leaves it out.

say: You give it a quadratic inequality, like $2x^2 - 5x - 12 \le 0$. It gives back the **interval** or intervals of $x$ where it is true.
The key idea: find the roots first, then use the shape of the graph. A U-shape is below the axis **between** the roots and above it **outside** them.

how.higher: Higher level asks it on Paper 1 as a 10-mark part inside a longer question: comparing two derivatives (2021) or finding the whole-number range where a model beats a target (2024).

steps.title: Factorise the quadratic
steps.say: Treat it as an equation first. Factorise $2x^2 - 5x - 12$ to find where it equals zero.

steps.title: Find the roots
steps.say: The roots are where each bracket is zero. They are the end points of the interval.

steps.title: Use the shape of the graph
steps.say: The $x^2$ term is positive, so the graph is a U. It dips below the axis between the roots. We want $\le 0$, so we want the part between $\hl{1}{-\tfrac{3}{2}}$ and $\hl{2}{4}$.

lines.text: Check $x = 0$: $-12 \le 0$, true. It lies inside the interval.

higher.tip: Get the inequality to compare with $0$ before you factorise. Writing a quadratic inequality with $0$ on one side is a step the marks are tied to.
Find the roots of the quadratic. Marks are given for the roots alone, even if the interval then goes wrong.
Do not treat it as a linear inequality. Working that does that earns very little.

higher.tip: Either an open or a closed end point is accepted for a $>$ inequality, so do not lose time worrying about it. Mark the roots clearly.

say: You give it a modulus inequality, like $|2x - 3| \ge 5$. It gives back the **interval(s)** of $x$ that make it true.
The key idea: $|\ \ |$ means distance from zero. A "less than" gives one interval between $-5$ and $5$, and a "greater than" gives two **outside** pieces joined by **or**.

how.higher: Higher level asks it on Paper 1 as a short part near the start of Question 1 or 2 (2016, 2020, 2025), worth 5 or 10 marks, and uses modulus equations in the same place (2021, 2023).

steps.title: Split into two inequalities
steps.say: A modulus that is at least $5$ means the inside is at least $5$ **or** at most $-5$. Write both.

steps.title: Solve the first one
steps.say: Add $3$ to both sides, then divide by $2$.

steps.title: Solve the second one
steps.say: Do the same with the other inequality. The sign stays the same way round, because $2$ is positive.

steps.title: Join the two pieces
steps.say: Both pieces are answers. Join them with **or**, never with and.

lines.text: Check $x = 5$: $|7| = 7 \ge 5$. It works. Check $x = 0$: $|-3| = 3$, not $\ge 5$. It is left out.

higher.tip: You may split into two linear inequalities or square both sides. Both routes earn full marks, so use the one you trust.
When you join the two pieces for a "less than" answer, write the word and (or the symbol $\cap$). Leaving it out loses a mark.

sources.quote: and or ∩ is not included in Method 1

higher.tip: A correct answer with no working still earns full marks, but one slip then leaves you with nothing. Show the two linear inequalities.
A graph is accepted if it shows the range on the $x$-axis. Listing only the natural numbers in the range earns high partial credit at most.

sources.quote: Note: use of natural numbers in range merits

say: You give it an inequality with $x$ in the bottom of a fraction, like $\frac{x+3}{x-1} \ge 2$. It gives back the **interval(s)** of $x$, with the value that makes the bottom zero left out.
The key idea: never multiply by the bottom itself, because it can be negative and flip the sign. Multiply by the bottom **squared**, which is never negative.

how.higher: Higher level has asked it once in this period, as a 10-mark part on Paper 1 in 2018 (Question 1(b)), where multiplying by the squared bottom turns it into a quadratic inequality.

steps.title: Multiply by the bottom squared
steps.say: Multiply both sides by $\hl{1}{(x-1)^2}$. It is always positive, so the sign stays the same way round.

steps.title: Make it a quadratic inequality
steps.say: Multiply out and move everything to one side, so the other side is $0$.

steps.title: Factorise and read off
steps.say: Factorise, then use the U-shape: it is below the axis between the roots.

steps.title: Leave out the bad value
steps.say: At $x = 1$ the bottom is zero, so the fraction does not exist. Remove $x = \hl{2}{1}$ from the interval.

higher.tip: Multiply through by the square of the bottom, as the scheme does. It is the first thing the marks look for.
Find the roots of the quadratic. Roots alone reach high partial credit.
Do not treat it as linear. That earns very little.
